editorial_contributions.text:
This paper gives a detailed and very instructive description of how the ninth Fermat number \(F_ 9= 2^{512}+1\) was factorized. Two new factors of \(F_ 9\), with 49 and 99 decimal digits, were found in the morning of June 15, 1990, after a concerted number crunching attack of approximately 700 workstations and a supercomputer over a period of four months. The method used was the number field sieve (NFS), which depends on arithmetic in an algebraic number field. For \(F_ 9\), this field was \(\mathbb{Q}({\root 5 \of {2}})\).


The paper starts with a survey of Fermat numbers and their place in number theory and history. Next a general class of methods for factoring \(n\) is discussed, based on finding integers \(x\) for which \(x^ 2\equiv 1\bmod n\), NFS being a special case. Using the actual prime factors of \(F_ 9\) it is explained why earlier attempts to factor it with other methods like the elliptic curve method have failed. After listing several basic facts from algebraic number theory, the authors describe the number field sieve, and how they applied it to \(F_ 9\). Next the actual sieving process is discussed, followed by the final step which involves the solution of a huge sparse \(226688\times 199203\) linear system over \(\mathbb{F}_ 2\) with an average of 50 nonzero elements per row. This system was reduced to a smaller system of size \(72413\times 72213\) by eliminating with certain sparse columns that cause fill-in only in certain so-called heavy columns. The final system was solved by means of ordinary Gaussian elimination on a 65536-processor Connection Machine at the expense of three hours CPU-time.


This decomposition of \(F_ 9\) into prime factors is to be considered a major achievement which was only possible by a combination of great skill in algebraic number theory, computational mathematics, and computer science.

title.title: The development of the number field sieve

editorial_contributions.text:
[For the entire collection see Zbl 0755.00009.]


Integer factoring algorithms are of great importance in cryptology. The paper presents a new technique that proved to be extremely useful, not only to speed-up well-known factoring algorithms, but also to introduce a new factoring algorithm. Until 1989 the best practical general purpose factoring algorithm was the quadratic sieve algorithm (mpqs, for short) with heuristic expected run time \(\exp((1+o(1))(\log n)^{1/2}(\log\log n)^{1/2})\). By this algorithm a record factorization of a 106 digit integer in 1989 was done. The mpqs works in two stages. In the first stage relations of the form \(\nu^ 2\equiv\prod p^{e_{\nu p}}\bmod n\) are collected, where \(e_{\nu p}\) is an integer \(\geq 0\) and the product ranges over the number \(-1\) and the primes less some bound \(B\). In the second stage one uses these relations to find integer solutions to \(x^ 2\equiv y^ 2\bmod n\). Each such solution has a good chance to lead to a factorization of \(n\) by computing \(\text{gcd}(n,x\pm y)\).


A new factoring algorithm, the so-called number field sieve (nfs) presented by the authors together with H. W. Lenstra and J. M. Pollard, was introduced as a special purpose algorithm which applies to \(n\) of the form \(r^ e-s\), where \(r\) is a small positive integer, and \(s\) is a non- zero integer of small absolute value. The heuristic expected run time of nfs is \(\exp((c+ o(1))(\log n)^{1/3}(\log\log n)^{2/3})\) with \(c=2(2/3)^{2/3}\). It is suspected that a generalization of nfs to integers of arbitrary form will run in time of the basic algorithm, though with a slightly bigger value for \(c\). The authors explain how to use two large primes with nfs. The practical consequences remain to be studied.

editorial_contributions.text:
In the present bibliography the author lists 14 items among which are six of this same volume, in approximately chronological order, of all literature that is directly related to the number field sieve.


1. \textit{J. M. Pollard}, Factoring with cubic integers (2), unpublished manuscript, 3 pages, December 1988. (This forms a footnote to the previous paper (this vol., pp. 4-10). It reports on the factorization of \(2^{144}-3\).)


2. \textit{D. M. Gordon}, Discrete logarithms in \(GF(p)\) using the number field sieve, SIAM J. Discrete Math. 6, 124-138 (1993; Zbl 0772.11046), prepublication: 15 pages, April 27, 1990.


3. \textit{L. M. Adleman}, Factoring numbers using singular integers, Proc. 23rd Annual ACM Symp. on Theory of Computing (STOC), New Orleans, May 6- 8, 1991, 64-71; prepublication: TR-20, Department of Computer Science, University of Southern California, 8 pages, September 4, 1990.


4. \textit{D. Coppersmith}, Modifications to the number field sieve, J. Cryptology 6, 169-180 (1993; see the review 11071 below), prepublication: IBM Research Report \#RC 16264, Yorktown Heights, New York, 16 pages, November 1990.


5. \textit{A. K. Lenstra}, \textit{H. W. Lenstra, jun.}, \textit{M. S. Manasse}, \textit{J. M. Pollard}, The factorization of the ninth Fermat number, Math. Comput. 61, 319-349 (1993; Zbl 0792.11055).


6. \textit{O. Schirokauer}, On pro-finite groups and on discrete logarithms, Ph. D. thesis, University of California, Berkeley, 68 pages, May 1992.
